1.1.1.title: 1.1.1 Non-text Content (A)
1.1.1.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.1.1 Non-text Content ensures accessibility for users with visual or hearing disabilities by providing text alternatives for meaningful images, icons, charts, graphs, and audio-only content (like podcasts). It also prevents decorative content from cluttering screen reader output.

All non-text content (visual and audio) must have a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, OR must be ignored if purely decorative.

1.2.1.title: 1.2.1 Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded) (A)
1.2.1.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.2.1 Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded) benefits users who have visual or hearing disabilities. The purpose of this SC is to make sure that any prerecorded time-based media that contains only audio or only video has an alternative that presents equivalent information.

Prerecorded audio-only media requires an alternative for time-based audio that presents equivalent information. Prerecorded video-only media requires an alternative or an audio track presenting equivalent information.

1.2.2.title: 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded) (A)
1.2.2.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded) primarily benefits users with hearing disabilities when watching prerecorded videos with audio content. Users who cannot hear will benefit from captions that are synchronized with the audio content.

Synchronized captions are provided for all prerecorded audio content in synchronized media. Captions must be synchronized, speakers must be identified, and important music/sound effects must be identified.

1.2.3.title: 1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded) (A)
1.2.3.html:
At Salesforce, we aim for WCAG level AA rather than A. Design/implementation of new prerecorded content must fall under the guidance in 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded).

When auditing existing content, test videos for bugs on audio descriptions or media alternatives under 1.2.5 rather than 1.2.3.

1.2.4.title: 1.2.4 Captions (Live) (AA)
1.2.4.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.2.4 Captions (Live) primarily benefits users with hearing disabilities when watching live/real-time videos with audio content. Users who cannot hear will benefit from captions that are synchronized with the audio content.

Synchronized captions are provided for all live synchronized media. If a live event is hosted on a platform that does not support native captioning, an external captioning link must be provided.

1.2.5.title: 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded) (AA)
1.2.5.html:
This SC benefits people who are blind or have visual impairments by ensuring there is an audio description of visual content in videos. Visual content needing an audio description can include important scene changes, text on the screen, charts or figures, or anything essential to fully understanding the video content.

An alternative audio description of the prerecorded video content is provided for synchronized media, either as part of the video's main audio track or a separate audio track.

1.3.1.title: 1.3.1 Info & Relationships (A)
1.3.1.html:
SC 1.3.1 Info & Relationships primarily benefits users with blindness or low vision. This SC ensures that relationships in content and information that are presented visually are also presented programmatically, so that assistive technology (AT) users can understand it.

This SC is very broad and covers data tables, form element grouping, visible labels, headings, lists, and other page structure and semantics.

1.3.2.title: 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence (A)
1.3.2.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence primarily benefits people with visual disabilities who use screen readers. If the visual layout is changed using CSS positioning or JavaScript but the code order stays the same, the screen reader might read things in an order that doesn't make sense.

When the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning, a correct reading sequence can be programmatically determined.

1.3.3.title: 1.3.3 Sensory Characteristics (A)
1.3.3.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.3.3 Sensory Characteristics deals with on-screen instructions. It benefits users who cannot perceive shape, size, visual placement, sound, or other characteristics that rely on a particular sense.

Any instructions provided for understanding and operating content do not rely only on sensory characteristics such as shape, color, size, visual location, orientation, or sound.

1.3.4.title: 1.3.4 Orientation (AA)
1.3.4.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.3.4 Orientation benefits users whose devices are mounted in a fixed orientation and cannot be freely rotated. Primary user groups that benefit include users with motor disabilities who have mounted their device to a wheelchair or other assistive equipment.

Content must not restrict its view and operation to a single display orientation, such as portrait or landscape, unless a specific orientation is essential.

1.3.5.title: 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose (AA)
1.3.5.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose primarily benefits users with dyslexia, memory impairments, cerebral palsy, motor neuron disease, stroke, cognitive disabilities, and mobility impairments. When the purpose of a form field collecting personal information is programmatically identified, browsers and assistive technologies can autofill fields.

The purpose of each input field that collects personal information about the user must be programmatically determinable using the HTML autocomplete attribute.

1.4.1.title: 1.4.1 Use of Color (A)
1.4.1.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.4.1 Use of Color primarily benefits people with color vision deficiency (colorblindness). If color alone is used to convey errors, changes in status, or other information, users who cannot perceive color will miss the information.

Ensure that color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element.

1.4.2.title: 1.4.2 Audio Control (A)
1.4.2.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.4.2 Audio Control primarily benefits blind screen reader users who rely on the audio output of their screen reader to interact with content online, and may not be able to hear the screen reader properly over other audio.

If any audio on a web page plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, a mechanism must be available to pause or stop the audio, or to control audio volume independently.

1.4.3.title: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (AA)
1.4.3.html:
People with visual impairments such as low vision or difficulty perceiving contrast benefit from Success Criterion (SC) 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum). Making sure there is sufficient contrast between text and its background helps written content be as accessible as possible.

Text must have at least a 4.5:1 contrast ratio with its background. Large text must have at least a 3:1 contrast ratio.

1.4.4.title: 1.4.4 Resize Text (AA)
1.4.4.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.4.4 Resize Text primarily benefits low vision users who need to increase the size of text content to be able to read it.

Users can resize text without assistive technology up to 200% without loss of information or functionality.

1.4.5.title: 1.4.5 Images of Text (AA)
1.4.5.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.4.5 Images of Text primarily benefits users with low vision or reading disabilities such as dyslexia who may need to alter the CSS of a page to be able to read the text.

If the same visual presentation can be made using text alone (with CSS), an image must not be used to present text.

1.4.10.title: 1.4.10 Reflow (AA)
1.4.10.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.4.10 Reflow covers reflow and responsive design. This benefits low vision users who need to increase the size of content to be able to perceive it.

Content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions for vertically scrolling content at 320 CSS pixels width.

1.4.11.title: 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (AA)
1.4.11.html:
People with visual impairments, such as low vision or difficulty perceiving contrast, benefit from Success Criterion (SC) 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast. Visual non-text information, such as icons, controls, or other graphical elements, can be essential for using digital products.

UI components, controls, and graphical objects conveying information must have at least a 3:1 contrast ratio with adjacent colors.

1.4.12.title: 1.4.12 Text Spacing (AA)
1.4.12.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.4.12 Text Spacing requires that users are able to adjust the spacing between words, letters, and paragraphs without content being lost or cut off. Users with reading disabilities such as dyslexia benefit most from this SC.

No loss of content or functionality occurs by setting line height to at least 1.5 times the font size, spacing following paragraphs to at least 2 times the font size, letter spacing to at least 0.12 times the font size, and word spacing to at least 0.16 times the font size.

1.4.13.title: 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (AA)
1.4.13.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus primarily benefits users with low vision, users of screen magnification software, users with cognitive or attention disabilities, and keyboard-only users.

When pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to appear, the content must be dismissible, hoverable, and persistent.

2.1.1.title: 2.1.1 Keyboard (A)
2.1.1.html:
Many user groups need to access content and functionality using the keyboard alone. For example, people without use of hands or users with motor disabilities may not be able to use a pointing device like a mouse.

Interactive controls must be accessible when using the keyboard alone without requiring specific timings for keystrokes. Custom controls must follow established and user-expected HTML keyboard behavior.

2.1.2.title: 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (A)
2.1.2.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap benefits users who use a keyboard to navigate through the web. This SC requires that the keyboard focus is not trapped in one spot.

If a user can use the keyboard to focus on a component, the user must also be able to move focus away from it using only the keyboard.

2.1.4.title: 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts (A)
2.1.4.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts is meant to reduce accidental activation of single-character keyboard shortcuts. It primarily benefits users who use the keyboard to interact with content online, and those who use voice dictation software.

If a keyboard shortcut is implemented using only letter, punctuation, number, or symbol characters, then it must be able to be turned off, remapped, or only active when that component has focus.

2.2.1.title: 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (A)
2.2.1.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable helps users who may encounter difficulties interacting with a system when the system imposes time limits or times out automatically.

Any time limit set by the content must allow users to turn it off, adjust it to at least 10 times the default, or extend it with at least 20 seconds warning.

2.2.2.title: 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (A)
2.2.2.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide has a goal of ensuring users aren't distracted or prevented from reading other content on the page due to moving content.

For moving, blinking, or scrolling content that starts automatically, lasts more than 5 seconds, and is presented in parallel with other content, there must be a mechanism to pause, stop, or hide it.

2.3.1.title: 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (A)
2.3.1.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold benefits users with photosensitive seizure disorders such as epilepsy. Flashing content can cause direct physical harm to some users in the form of seizures.

In Salesforce, no flashing content is permitted. This is the simplest way to meet this requirement. Any bug under this SC is automatically a P0.

2.4.1.title: 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (A)
2.4.1.html:
Bypass blocks and skip links allow users to skip keyboard focus over large pieces of content that repeats across pages, such as navigation sections appearing at the top of every page.

A mechanism is available to bypass blocks of content that are repeated on multiple web pages. Skip links must be included that allow users to skip past content that repeats across pages.

2.4.2.title: 2.4.2 Page Titled (A)
2.4.2.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.4.2 Page Titled benefits primarily screen reader users who cannot visually scan a page to see its purpose. Screen readers announce the page title first when a page loads or when the user navigates to a new tab.

Each page must have a descriptive title provided in the head of the page that is specific enough to distinguish the page's purpose from other pages.

2.4.3.title: 2.4.3 Focus Order (A)
2.4.3.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.4.3 Focus Order benefits sighted keyboard users, screen reader users, and users with low vision who use screen magnifiers. The focus order for interactive page elements must be intuitive and follow a visually logical reading order.

The focus order must preserve meaning and operability. When a button launches a modal dialog, after closing the modal, focus should return to the element that launched the dialog or to the next logical step.

2.4.4.title: 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) (A)
2.4.4.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context) benefits all users, motor-impaired users, and users with cognitive disabilities who rely on clear, predictable link text.

The purpose of each link must be determinable from either the link text alone, or the link text together with its programmatically determined context.

2.4.5.title: 2.4.5 Multiple Ways (AA)
2.4.5.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.4.5 Multiple Ways benefits users of various assistive technologies and users with cognitive disabilities. Different people benefit from different methods of navigating content online.

More than one way must be provided for users to locate a web page within a set of web pages, such as links between pages, navigation menus, or site search.

2.4.6.title: 2.4.6 Headings and Labels (AA)
2.4.6.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.4.6 Headings and Labels benefits all users, particularly those with visual or cognitive disabilities, by requiring that any headings or labels used to identify content are clear and descriptive.

If headings and labels exist on the page, they clearly describe the topic or purpose.

2.4.7.title: 2.4.7 Focus Visible (AA)
2.4.7.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.4.7 Focus Visible benefits sighted keyboard users, users with low vision who use screen magnifiers, and users with attention limitations or short-term memory limitations.

When any user interface component receives keyboard focus, there must be a visible indicator that shows which component is focused.

2.4.11.title: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (AA)
2.4.11.html:
Success criterion (SC) 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured benefits sighted keyboard-only users when content such as overlays, menus, etc. appears in front of interactive elements.

When a UI component receives keyboard focus, the component must not be completely hidden due to other page content. The focused item must be at least partially visible.

2.5.1.title: 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures (A)
2.5.1.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures ensures that functionality operated using multipoint or path-based gestures can also be operated with a single pointer without a path-based gesture.

All functionality that uses multipoint gestures or path-based gestures must also be operable with a single pointer using a non-path-based action.

2.5.2.title: 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation (A)
2.5.2.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation benefits users who may accidentally activate controls with a pointer. When functions execute only on the up-event, users can cancel an accidental activation by moving the pointer away before releasing.

For functionality operated using a single pointer, the down-event must not be used to execute any part of the function, or completion must be on the up-event with cancellation or undo available.

2.5.3.title: 2.5.3 Label in Name (A)
2.5.3.html:
When visible text labels are the same as their accessible (programmatic) name, users of speech input software can interact with those controls by speaking the visible label.

For user interface components with labels that include text or images of text, the programmatic name contains the text that is presented visually.

2.5.4.title: 2.5.4 Motion Actuation (A)
2.5.4.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.5.4 Motion Actuation benefits users who may not be able to use device functionality that relies on movement of the device or a body part.

Functionality that can be operated by device motion or user motion can also be operated by UI components, and responding to the motion can be disabled.

2.5.7.title: 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA)
2.5.7.html:
The purpose of Success Criterion (SC) 2.5.7 Dragging Movements is to provide an alternative for people using a pointing device who have difficulty with dragging dexterity.

All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation must have an alternative that can be achieved by a single pointer action without dragging.

2.5.8.title: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA)
2.5.8.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) improves accessibility for users with motor impairments. When buttons or controls are too close together, it can be difficult to accurately click or tap the correct control.

Interactive controls must be a minimum of 24 by 24 CSS pixels in size, or surrounded by enough space so that they have at least a 24 by 24 CSS pixel circle around the interactive area.

3.1.1.title: 3.1.1 Language of Page (A)
3.1.1.html:
Success criterion (SC) 3.1.1 Language of Page benefits screen reader users such as individuals who are blind or low vision. Screen readers use different voices depending on the language spoken.

The page's primary language must be defined using the lang attribute on the html element.

3.1.2.title: 3.1.2 Language of Parts (AA)
3.1.2.html:
Success criterion (SC) 3.1.2 Language of Parts benefits screen reader users. Screen readers use different voices depending on the language spoken. Ensuring that content outside the main language of the page is marked up correctly allows screen readers to pronounce words correctly.

The language of any content outside the page's primary language must be defined using the lang attribute on the parent element.

3.2.1.title: 3.2.1 On Focus (A)
3.2.1.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.2.1 On Focus specifically deals with unexpected changes that occur when the user moves keyboard focus to an interactive element. This SC benefits people with visual disabilities, cognitive limitations, and motor impairments.

When any user interface component receives focus, it does not initiate a change of context.

3.2.2.title: 3.2.2 On Input (A)
3.2.2.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.2.2 On Input specifically deals with unexpected changes that occur when the user enters data into a field. This SC benefits people with visual disabilities, cognitive limitations, and motor impairments.

Changing the setting of any user interface component does not automatically cause a change of context unless the user has been advised of the behavior ahead of time.

3.2.3.title: 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation (AA)
3.2.3.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation primarily benefits users with cognitive disabilities, low vision, and motor disabilities. When navigation mechanisms that repeat across pages appear in the same relative order, users can build a reliable mental model.

Navigational mechanisms that are repeated on multiple pages within a set of pages must occur in the same relative order each time they are repeated.

3.2.4.title: 3.2.4 Consistent Identification (AA)
3.2.4.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.2.4 Consistent Identification benefits users with cognitive disabilities, visual disabilities, and motor impairments. When components that perform the same function are labeled consistently across pages, users can build reliable mental models.

Components that have the same functionality within a set of web pages must be identified consistently.

3.2.6.title: 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A)
3.2.6.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.2.6 Consistent Help primarily benefits users with cognitive disabilities who rely on being able to locate help in a predictable location.

If a web page contains help mechanisms and that mechanism is repeated across multiple pages within a set of web pages, it must appear in the same relative order on each page where it appears.

3.3.1.title: 3.3.1 Error Identification (A)
3.3.1.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.3.1 Error Identification benefits all users. Primary user groups that benefit include those with cognitive disabilities, motor disabilities, and individuals with visual disabilities.

If an input error is automatically detected, the item that is in error is identified and the error is described to the user in text.

3.3.2.title: 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (A)
3.3.2.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions benefits all users, particularly those with cognitive or learning disabilities and users with motor issues.

When user input is required on a form, labels or instructions are provided. Labels for individual fields must be visible, required fields must be identified, and placeholder text alone cannot be the only method of providing labels.

3.3.3.title: 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (AA)
3.3.3.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.3.3 Error Suggestion benefits all users. Primary user groups that benefit include those with cognitive disabilities, motor disabilities, and individuals with visual disabilities.

If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then the suggestions are provided to the user, unless it would jeopardize security or purpose.

3.3.4.title: 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) (AA)
3.3.4.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.3.4 Error Prevention benefits all users. Primary user groups that benefit include those with cognitive disabilities, motor disabilities, and individuals with visual disabilities.

For pages that cause legal commitments, financial transactions, user-controlled data to be modified or deleted, or test responses to be submitted, the submission must be reversible, checked for errors, or confirmed before finalizing.

3.3.7.title: 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A)
3.3.7.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.3.7 Redundant Entry helps users with cognitive disabilities and motor disabilities who struggle to re-enter previously provided information.

Information previously entered by or provided to the user that is required again in the same process must either be auto-populated or available for the user to select.

3.3.8.title: 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (AA)
3.3.8.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication primarily benefits users with cognitive disabilities and motor disabilities who may find it difficult or impossible to complete cognitive function tests as a condition of authentication.

A cognitive function test must not be required to complete any step in an authentication process unless an alternative method is available, a mechanism assists completion, or the test involves recognizing objects or user-provided content.

4.1.2.title: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A)
4.1.2.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value benefits users of assistive technology such as screen readers or voice dictation software. Ensuring all components have programmatically assigned names, roles, states, and values means users of AT can properly interpret and use controls.

All UI components must have programmatically determined names and roles. Where appropriate, states, properties, or values set by users must be programmatically available and include notification of changes to assistive technology.

4.1.3.title: 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA)
4.1.3.html:
Success Criterion (SC) 4.1.3 Status Messages benefits users of assistive technology, particularly blind and low vision users of screen readers, by ensuring that they are informed about status messages that are displayed visually.

When a status message is displayed visually, the message must be announced via screen reader without receiving focus.
